chapter: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
title: Leroy Snakebite White, schooled musician and arranger
summary: Howard recalls Snake White as an East Coast trumpeter who wrote hard arrangements; Collette says he helped young players learn to read.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. We're back to the trombone player, can't think (inaudible).
Trombone.
(Inaudible.) Snake White. Do you know
that name? Oh, yeah.
Leroy "Snakebite" White
Leroy Snakebite. Do you know where he was from?
No.
Back East. He came from back East, and played trumpet.
Right. Some very hard arrangements and in some very strange keys, right?
Very, very hard.
Okay, what do you know about this man? He had his own band and what else did he do?
Well, he had his own band and he played with me.
Was he a good man, though?
Excuse me, nervousness.
That's all right, just (inaudible). Was he a good trumpet player?
Oh, yeah.
Seemed to be a schooled musician.
Yeah, a schooled musician, that's what he was, very much a schooled musician.
Snake was -- a terrific guy. He also helped a bunch of the young players, like Jack Kelso
Chico Hamilton, (inaudible), Mingus and me.
Yep.
Because he'd write arrangements and he needed somebody to read them. He learned to read by playing his music in D, A, a lot of sharps, a lot of sharps on the alto saxophone.
Yeah, he did that. He did so many things. People did so many things that it's hard to keep up with them. Everybody was trying hard. They don't try no more.
